catalog_quote: [Trager 1946 p.189, sec. 2:221] Stress is a phonemic feature of Taos, existing in the form of loud stress, medial stress, and weak stress. The first two may be combined with any one of the three tones. That stress as such is phonemic is indicated by the fact that no rules on a phonemic level can be devised determining the place of the stressed syllables in a word, and such rules as can be laid down for certain morphological combinations are either very complicated or show many exceptions. There are not many instances of words distinguished by the position of loud stress alone (that is, without accompanying tone differences), but there are some ... Moreover, many nouns vary the stress patterns as between singular and plural absolute forms, and these changes are as important to correct apprehension of the forms as those in the suffixes. ... Medial stress is found only where a loud stress …

sources.citation: Hoijer, Harry and Dozier, E. P. (1949). The phonemes of Tewa, Santa Clara dialect. International Journal of American Linguistics 15. pp. 139-144.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: The work describes the Santa Clara dialect of Tewa (Glottolog tewa1260), a different Kiowa-Tanoan language, not Taos or Northern Tiwa; its statements cannot be transferred to nort1550. Note also that the listed open_url http://wals.info/refdb/record/360 resolves to the WALS record Holmer-1949d (Goajiro phonology), a wrong record; the correct WALS record is Hoijer-and-Dozier-1949, and the article itself was read from the public archive.org copy of IJAL 15(3).

Trager 1968 describes a Picuris singular/plural distinction based on stress and nasalization.

sources.note: The only competing primary analysis of Taos suprasegmentals: three tones (high/falling/low) with stress as an independent system (Sutton 2014 pp.161, 407); bears on whether Taos should stay lexical stress or be flagged tonal-OR-pitch accent.
